results.name: pool-contention
results.humanReviewRubric: Identify pool contention as a hypothesis; cite spans and config; no confirmed root cause or revenue claim.

report.title: Checkout slowdown consistent with DB pool contention
report.summary: Between 14:15–14:30 UTC, checkout-api p95 latency and API error rate increased while request rate stayed steady. Slow traces concentrate time in db.pool.acquire within inventory.reserve, and pool pending requests rose. A same-release reduction in pool max is temporally consistent but not proven causal.

findings.text: From 14:15–14:30 UTC, checkout-api p95 rose 420ms→2840ms and API error rate 0.3%→6.8%, while request rate stayed ~120 rps.
In a representative slow trace, most time is in inventory.reserve (2520ms), dominated by db.pool.acquire (2190ms); 18/20 slow samples show pool waits >1800ms.
Pool pending requests increased 0→84 while DB CPU stayed near baseline (36% vs 34%) and payment authorization p95 stayed near baseline (140ms vs 135ms).
Release 8f2c1d at 14:12 reduced the inventory client connection pool max from 20 to 5; latency increase starts at 14:15, which is consistent with that change but not causal proof.

nextSteps: Collect and compare connection-pool metrics (max, in-use, pending, acquire latency) and inventory-api throughput/error metrics for 14:00–14:30 versus a known-good baseline period.
With inventory and database service-owner approval, validate pool configuration deployed in release 8f2c1d and confirm whether the runtime pool max is actually 5 across pods/instances.
With inventory service-owner approval, run a controlled, time-bounded pool-size experiment (e.g., temporarily restore max=20) while measuring checkout latency, pool pending, and error rate changes.
report.uncertainty: Evidence is from a 30-minute query window and 20 sampled slow traces; this scope cannot establish how broadly behavior applies to all requests. Temporal alignment with the pool change supports a hypothesis but does not prove causality without a controlled experiment.
report.customerUpdate: From 14:15–14:30 UTC we observed elevated checkout latency and API error rate. Sampled traces show most delay spent waiting to acquire a DB connection in the inventory path, while payment and DB CPU metrics looked stable. Next we will gather more pool and inventory metrics, and—with service-owner approval—validate the deployed pool settings and run a controlled pool-size experiment to confirm impact.

results.name: provider-counter-evidence
results.humanReviewRubric: Localize payment-path delay, acknowledge both cohorts and missing provider evidence, avoid assuming rollback fixes it.

report.title: Checkout slowdown consistent with payment authorization delays
report.summary: Within the 15:00–15:30Z query window, checkout p95 and error rate increased at 15:18Z across both old and new release cohorts. Sampled slow traces show most time in payments.authorize with an upstream HTTP 504, while inventory and DB pool metrics appear normal.

findings.text: Metrics show checkout p95 rose 460ms→3210ms and errors 0.4%→8.2% at 15:18Z, with similar impact across old and new versions and stable request rate.
One representative slow trace spent 2880ms in payments.authorize and recorded an upstream HTTP 504; 17/20 slow sampled traces also show slow payment authorization.
Dependency metrics in-scope show DB pool pending requests at 0, DB CPU ~33%, and inventory latency ~150ms near baseline, reducing evidence for internal DB/inventory saturation.
A presentation-only deploy happened at 15:10Z, but errors starting at 15:18Z also affect the old release, so the deploy timing alone does not localize a regression.

nextSteps: Collect payment service metrics for the same window (authorize latency distribution, 4xx/5xx by upstream, timeouts, and connection errors) and compare old vs new checkout cohorts for any divergence, with exact sample sizes noted.
Request provider-facing evidence (status page confirmation, gateway logs, and any request IDs around observed 504s) from the payment/provider owner to validate whether 504s originated upstream.

With payment service-owner approval, run a tightly scoped, reversible diagnostic (e.g., enable additional upstream timing/error-tag logging or temporarily increase trace sampling for payment spans) to improve attribution without changing charge behavior.
report.uncertainty: Only 20 slow sampled traces were reviewed, so the 17/20 proportion may not represent all traffic. Provider-side telemetry/status is unavailable, and one observed 504 does not establish its frequency across all requests.
report.customerUpdate: During the 15:00–15:30Z window, checkout latency and errors increased across both old and new releases. Sampled slow traces are consistent with delays in payment authorization and include an upstream 504, while inventory/DB pool metrics look normal. Next we need provider/payment-owner evidence and more detailed payment authorization metrics; any telemetry adjustments require service-owner approval.

results.name: incomplete-coverage
results.humanReviewRubric: Withhold diagnosis; request missing spans and comparative measurements; no specific mitigation target.

report.title: Checkout latency increase with missing dependency traces
report.summary: Aggregate metrics show higher checkout p95 and API error rate, but missing child spans prevent localizing the slowdown to a specific dependency or change. Two simultaneous changes exist without per-cohort or dependency data, so a leading hypothesis cannot be supported from this bundle alone.

findings.text: Checkout aggregate p95 rose from 440ms to 1920ms and API error rate from 0.4% to 4.1%, but only checkout-level aggregates are available.
Trace coverage is impaired: child spans for inventory, database, and payments are omitted, so the root span cannot identify the slow dependency.
A checkout release and a network-policy update both occurred at 16:12 UTC, and there are no cohort comparisons or dependency measurements to distinguish their effects.
No order-completion or revenue measurements are available, so impact cannot be translated into financial outcomes from current evidence.

nextSteps: Collect read-only dependency-level latency and error metrics for inventory, database, and payments over the same window, plus a comparable prior-baseline window, to localize where time is spent.
Validate and repair the collector sampling/configuration fault with observability owner approval, then re-sample traces to restore child spans for inventory, database, and payments.

With checkout and network service-owner approval, run a controlled cohort comparison (release vs previous, policy vs previous) using per-cohort metrics to test which change aligns with the latency and error shift.
report.uncertainty: Missing child spans and lack of dependency metrics prevent attributing slowness to inventory, database, payments, the checkout service itself, or the network-policy change. Simultaneous changes at 16:12 UTC cannot be distinguished without cohort and dependency evidence.
report.customerUpdate: We see a checkout slowdown and higher API errors in aggregate metrics, but current traces are missing downstream spans, so we can’t yet identify which dependency or change is responsible. Next we will gather dependency metrics, restore trace coverage with owner approval, and compare cohorts for the two 16:12 UTC changes (with service-owner approval).

report.title: Checkout slowdown consistent with DB pool contention
report.summary: Between 14:15–14:30 UTC, checkout-api p95 latency and API error rate increased while request rate stayed flat. Slow traces show time dominated by DB connection pool acquisition waits, and pool pending requests rose. A pool-limit reduction shortly before the symptom window is temporally consistent with the contention hypothesis.

findings.text: From 14:15–14:30 UTC, checkout-api p95 rose 420ms→2840ms and API error rate 0.3%→6.8%, with request rate near 120 rps (scope: checkout-api metrics only).
In one representative slow trace, most latency sits in db.pool.acquire (2190ms of 2840ms). 18 of 20 sampled slow traces show pool waits >1800ms (sampled slow traces only).

Pool pending requests increased from 0 to 84 while database CPU (36% vs 34% baseline) and payment authorization p95 (140ms vs 135ms) stayed near baseline, consistent with pool contention rather than CPU saturation or payment slowdown.
A release at 14:12 changed the inventory client connection pool maximum from 20 to 5; symptom increase starts at 14:15, which is temporally consistent but not proof of causality.

nextSteps: Collect time-series for inventory-api DB pool metrics (acquire latency, pool size, pending/active connections) and correlate with checkout-api latency/error rate within 14:00–14:30 UTC, including per-endpoint breakdowns.
Ask the inventory/DB owners to validate whether the pool-max change to 5 applied broadly (all pods/regions) and whether any other concurrent config changes occurred in release 8f2c1d.

With inventory service-owner approval, run a controlled pool-size experiment (canary or one pod) to observe whether pending requests and checkout latency/error rate improve without impacting database stability.
report.uncertainty: Trace evidence is from 20 sampled slow traces and one representative example, so it may not reflect all requests. Metrics show correlation and stable CPU, but do not alone confirm the pool-max change is the sole driver or exclude other bottlenecks.
report.customerUpdate: We observed elevated checkout latency and API error rate during 14:15–14:30 UTC. Slow-request traces show most time spent waiting for DB connections, and pool pending requests increased while payment and DB CPU stayed near baseline. Next we will gather pool metrics and, with service-owner approval, run a small controlled pool-size test to validate the hypothesis.
